extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, students of literature, and readers evaluating poetic style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating (and composing) metrical poetry: when metre is appropriate, how poetic language should differ from prose, how passion and volition should combine, and what kinds of diction, images, and figures are permissible or vicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential difference between prose and metrical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be an essential difference between the language of prose and of metrical composition; in many important senses the language appropriate to one will be unfit for the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge argues from practice (best poets, all ages and countries) that a real and essential difference ought to exist; readers and critics should expect such a difference and judge whether a passage truly suits metrical form or is merely prose dressed as verse. Examples cited: many passages in great poets would be harmed if every poetic peculiarity were deleted; conversely, some prose pieces would not be improved by conversion to rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre should be accompanied by a general language of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: As the elements of metre owe their existence to a state of increased excitement, the metre itself should be accompanied by the general language of excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrical works legitimately admit a greater use of picturesque and vivifying language than prose. The critic should look for a heightened diction appropriate to the excited state that produced metre. Without that excited diction metre becomes merely a stimulant without suitable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traces of present volition must be discernible in metrical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the elements of metre were organized by an act of will for the purpose of pleasure, traces of present volition (conscious artistic purpose) should throughout the metrical language be proportionably discernible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's conscious shaping and purpose should be evident — not merely spontaneous utterance. Critics should look for signs that the poet consciously adapts language and form to produce combined pleasure and emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union (interpenetration) of passion and volition
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be not only a partnership but a union — an interpenetration of passion (spontaneous impulse) and of voluntary purpose — manifested in the frequency and kinds of poetic forms and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good metrical language shows both genuine emotional impulse and the controlling direction of the poet's art: frequent picturesque and vivifying turns of speech that feel both born of passion and shaped by will. Critics should reject passages where passion and volition are merely juxtaposed rather than organically united.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate subject-matter (food) must match metre's stimulative effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre acts as a stimulant of attention and vivacity; where correspondent food and appropriate matter are not provided for the attention and feelings thus roused, there will be disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the subject, thought, and matter of the poem can sustain the heightened attention metre creates. Metre is like yeast: effective only when proportionally combined with fitting material. Examples/anti-patterns: metre that excites expectations but lacks substance (compared to 'leaping in the dark').

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre is conditional; thoughts and expressions must be appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of metre is conditional and dependent on the appropriateness of the thoughts and expressions to which the metrical form is superadded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge metre in isolation: evaluate whether the diction, images, and ideas are appropriate to be intensified by metre. Meter alone cannot justify incoherent or inappropriate diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language must match the specific passion being expressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry always implies passion (an excited state of the feelings and faculties), and as every passion has its proper pulse, so it will have characteristic modes of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should evaluate whether the modes of diction, figures, and syntax correspond to the particular emotion (love, fear, rage, jealousy, etc.) being expressed. Poetic style should be adapted to the kind and degree of feeling, not generic or mismatched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and harmonious adjustment of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: All the parts of an organized whole must be assimilated to the more important and essential parts; composition seeks unity by harmonious adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poems for structural harmony — elements (tone, diction, meter, imagery) should be assimilated to central, essential parts of the poem. Coleridge invokes the imitative arts' demand that either the same pervade throughout radically different parts or difference be adjusted uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incongruous or confused imagery and personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines that convey incongruous images or confuse cause and effect (e.g., 'And reddening Phoebus lifts his golden fire') are bad not because they are unlike prose but because they convey incongruous imagery and lack good sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate imagery for internal congruity and sensible relations. Avoid personifications or mythological figures that create confusion of logical relation; judge whether such usages are accidental/hackneyed or defensible by context and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosaic diction in poetry (meter must not be only to the eye)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if sense is good, language correct, and subject treated with feeling, a style may be justly blamable as prosaic if the words and their order would naturally belong in prose rather than metrical composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether lines can be transcribed into prose (or into blank verse printed as prose) without loss; if so, metre may be merely visual. Examples: Daniel's 'prosaic Daniel' and blank verse that reads indistinguishably as prose. Anti-pattern: successive lines that an ear cannot recognize as verse when read as prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency/intensity of figures should be proportionate to the emotion and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The frequency of forms of speech (figures, epithets) originally offspring of passion but now children of power should be greater than in prose only where emotion is voluntarily encouraged and used for pleasurable excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the density of figurative language against the degree of passion and the poet's conscious purpose. Excessive ornament without sufficient emotional justification is vicious; appropriate increase in frequency is justified when there is a prior, understood companionship between poet and reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction must be guided by principles (grammar, logic, psychology, knowledge, taste), not caprice
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's style should be regulated by principles — grammar, logic, psychology, and practical knowledge — which, when governed by good sense and habit, become Taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should expect rule-governed judgments about diction and style rather than arbitrary whims. Evaluate whether a poet's choices reflect conscious knowledge and taste rather than mere eccentricity or fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine poetic language arises from imaginative principles rather than external mechanical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of the Imagination are the powers of growth and production; if poetry were reduced to rules from without it would become a mechanical art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While style should be informed by principles, authentic poetic diction is ultimately born of imaginative discrimination and instinct. Critics should beware of reducing poetry to prescriptive formulae; seek signs of inner imaginative authority distinguishing genuine expressions from mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical/contextual acceptability of archaic or learned images
rubrics_metrics.description: Hackneyed or mythological personifications (e.g., 'Phoebus') may be accidental faults depending on the age and accepted poetic machinery; what is puerile in a modern poet can be pleasurable in older poets whose context made such imagery appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating diction, account for historical taste and learned tradition. Distinguish between genuinely puerile, anachronistic usage in a contemporary poet and the cultured revival of traditional imagery in earlier writers (Petrarch, Chaucer, Spenser).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre may have functional/mnemonic value but should not be used for that alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre (and alliteration/rhyme) historically assisted recollection and preservation (e.g., ballads), but this functional value is not by itself sufficient reason for choosing metre if the matter and diction do not warrant it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether metre serves a purpose (mnemonic, performative, affective) for the poem's subject; do not accept metre solely because of traditional or mnemonic reasons when the poem's material would be better served in prose.
